title: The big lookout: year one close
hook: stories, practices, the Psalms and Mark, the mystics, the Catechism: a whole landscape seen from here
tomorrow: year two opens: a library, not a book

segments.voice: Yesterday, prayer is relationship: the raising of mind and heart to God. Your line was lift up your heart. When did you lift yours, even once? Today, the last day of year one. Day three hundred thirty-one.

An hour into the trail, it's still all roots and rocks and your own boots, head down, one switchback after another. You stop noticing how high you've come. Then the trees open, there's a wooden rail and a bench, and suddenly the whole valley is below you: the river you crossed at the start, the ridge you thought would never end, the parking lot, tiny now. You didn't see any of it while you were climbing. You only see it from here. That's today. Three hundred thirty-one days, and a bench at the top of year one. Sit down. Look.
screen: `HEAD DOWN, ONE SWITCHBACK AT A TIME.` → `THE TREES OPEN.` → `A BENCH AT THE TOP OF YEAR ONE.`

segments.voice: First, where you started. Camp one was first words: grace, the sign of the cross, the Mass, Mary, the saints, the rosary, confession, Sunday, the Our Father, Lent, Easter, the Eucharist, mercy, the Psalms. Camp two was the stories: the child, the parables, Holy Week, the cross and the morning, the fire of Pentecost, the saints one by one. Camp three was the practices: the body at prayer, the Mass scene by scene, the rosary, the seven sacraments, confession up close, adoration, the Church's year. Second, the text itself. The Psalms, whose words Jesus cries out from the cross in Mark, then the Gospel of Mark straight through, ending at an empty tomb and a young man saying he goes before you. Third, the depths. Ways of praying: lectio divina, the examen, the Jesus Prayer, a friar at his pots and pans. Teresa's crystal castle with God at the center. John of the Cross and his dark night. Thomas Merton on a Louisville street corner. Then the Catechism, a map and not a wall, all the way to yesterday: prayer is relationship. Fourth, a lookout in the Bible. At the end of Deuteronomy, Moses climbs Mount Nebo, and God shows him the whole land at once: Gilead as far as Dan, Naphtali, Ephraim and Manasseh, Judah to the far sea, and the plain of Jericho, the city of palm trees. The text is honest: he sees it with his eyes, but he doesn't cross over. Others will walk it. A lookout isn't the end of the walking. It's where you finally see what you've been walking through. And Catholics have a short, old answer for a moment like that. At Mass, after the readings and again at the very end, the people say: thanks be to God. In Latin, Deo gratias. Tomorrow the trail goes on: year two opens the Bible itself, in order.
screen: `FIRST WORDS, STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `THE PSALMS, THEN MARK STRAIGHT THROUGH.` · `THE MYSTICS, THEN THE CATECHISM.` · `MOSES SEES THE WHOLE LAND FROM NEBO.` · then, large: `DEO GRATIAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look back over your year and give thanks. Settle, and breathe. Let the year come back to you, not in order, just as it comes. One word that stuck. One story you told someone. One day you almost skipped and didn't. One day you did skip, and came back anyway. Don't grade any of it. Just look, the way you'd look from a bench at the top of a trail. Then, for each thing that comes, say thanks. If you pray, you can use the old words from the Mass, thanks be to God. If you don't, a plain thank you is enough. The bell holds the time.
The big lookout. The end of year one: the stories, the practices, the Psalms and Mark, the mystics and the Catechism, seen all at once from one bench. Today's word.
Your line: you know this country now. Today, tell one person one thing you learned this year, the way you'd point out a landmark from the top. Day three hundred thirty-one.

screen: `DAY 331 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR TWO OPENS: A LIBRARY, NOT A BOOK.`

howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics answer "Thanks be to God" (Deo gratias) after the first readings and at the dismissal, and some parishes sing the Te Deum, an ancient hymn of thanksgiving, on the last day of the calendar year.

options: you walk down and cross over into it.

fork.reveal: he sees it with his eyes, and the text is honest: he doesn't cross over. others will walk it. the lookout shows the whole land at once.

notes: Year-one close: the camp-by-camp look back lists camp one's words and the parts of camps two to five as they appear in the index; confirm the list reads fairly and nothing central is missing.
Deuteronomy 34:1–4 paraphrased (Gilead unto Dan, the plain of Jericho, the city of palm trees; Moses sees but does not cross over). Confirm the paraphrase against the Douay-Rheims.

Deo gratias: in the current Roman Rite the people answer 'Thanks be to God' after the first and second readings (not after the Gospel) and at the dismissal. The script says 'after the readings and again at the very end'; confirm this is precise enough.
howItsDone mentions the Te Deum sung on the last day of the calendar year (December 31) in many parishes; confirm the custom is described accurately.
Latin pronunciation given in Church (Italianate) style.
Day 331's word 'The big lookout' is the title's head per the index; kept exactly.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer opens 'You know that kind of hike'; 'the Psalms, the prayer book Jesus prayed' (unsourced) changed to the Psalm words Jesus cries from the cross in Mark 15:34 (added to sources); the Nebo list now follows Deuteronomy 34:1–3 (Naphtali, Ephraim and Manasseh, Judah) and treats 'the city of palm trees' as Jericho, not a separate place; howItsDone's 'many parishes' sing the Te Deum softened to 'some'.
